q: Inhaled air is filtered, warmed and moistened mainly in the:
o: Larynx
Bronchioles
Nasal cavity
Alveoli
x: The nasal cavity is lined with hairs, mucus and a rich blood supply, so it filters, warms and moistens air before it goes deeper. The alveoli are for gas exchange, not air conditioning.

q: The hairs and mucus lining the nasal cavity mainly function to:
o: Secrete surfactant to keep the airways open
Produce sound during speech
Trap dust particles and microbes in the inhaled air
Exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide with the blood
x: Nasal hairs and sticky mucus catch dust, pollen and microbes so cleaner air reaches the lungs. Sound comes from the larynx and gas exchange happens in the alveoli.

q: Inhaled air is warmed and moistened in the nasal cavity mainly because its lining has:
o: A layer of pleural fluid
Thick bands of skeletal muscle
C-shaped rings of cartilage
A rich blood supply and a moist mucous membrane
x: Blood vessels just under the moist mucous membrane give heat to the air, and the mucus adds water vapour. Cartilage rings belong to the trachea and pleural fluid surrounds the lungs.

q: The common passage shared by both food and air is the:
o: Pharynx
Larynx
Trachea
Oesophagus
x: The pharynx (throat) carries air to the larynx and food to the oesophagus. The larynx and trachea carry only air; the oesophagus carries only food.

q: During swallowing, food is prevented from entering the larynx because:
o: The epiglottis covers the glottis
The vocal cords close the trachea from below
The cricoid cartilage blocks the pharynx
The bronchi constrict
x: When we swallow, the larynx moves up and the flap-like epiglottis closes over the glottis, so food passes into the oesophagus. The vocal cords produce sound and the cricoid is a ring of the larynx wall.

q: The larynx is called the voice box because it contains the:
o: Vocal cords
Bronchial glands
Tonsils
Olfactory receptors
x: The vocal cords stretched across the larynx vibrate to produce sound. Olfactory receptors for smell are in the nasal cavity.

q: Sound is produced in the larynx when:
o: The cartilage rings of the trachea vibrate
The diaphragm vibrates against the lungs
Exhaled air makes the stretched vocal cords vibrate
Inhaled air makes the epiglottis vibrate
x: Voice is produced as air breathed out passes between the tightened vocal cords and makes them vibrate. The epiglottis only guards the glottis during swallowing.

q: The 'Adam's apple' seen at the front of the neck is formed by the:
o: Cricoid cartilage of the larynx
Epiglottis
First ring of the trachea
Thyroid cartilage of the larynx
x: The largest cartilage of the larynx, the thyroid cartilage, projects forward as the Adam's apple, especially in males. The cricoid is a smaller ring lying below it.

q: The trachea wall contains C-shaped rings of cartilage. Their main function is to:
o: Secrete mucus to trap dust
Keep the trachea open so it does not collapse
Move mucus up towards the pharynx
Allow gas exchange through the wall
x: The cartilage rings support the trachea wall so the airway stays open during breathing. Mucus is made by goblet cells and moved by cilia, not by cartilage.

q: The cartilage rings of the trachea are incomplete at the back, where the trachea touches the oesophagus. This arrangement allows:
o: The vocal cords to move freely
The oesophagus to expand when swallowed food passes down
Gas exchange to take place through the back wall of the trachea
The trachea to collapse fully during inspiration
x: The open part of each C faces the oesophagus, so a mass of food can bulge the oesophagus forward slightly. The front and sides stay rigid to keep the airway open; the trachea is not a gas-exchange surface.

q: The inner lining of the trachea consists of:
o: Keratinised stratified epithelium
Ciliated epithelium with mucus-secreting goblet cells
Smooth muscle with no epithelium
A single layer of flat squamous cells
x: The trachea is lined by ciliated (pseudostratified columnar) epithelium containing goblet cells. Goblet cells make mucus to trap particles and the cilia sweep it away. Flat squamous cells line the alveoli.

q: Dust trapped in mucus inside the trachea and bronchi is removed by:
o: Diffusion of the dust into the blood
Digestion of the dust by surfactant
The beating of cilia, which moves the mucus up to the pharynx
Contraction of the cartilage rings
x: Cilia beat in one direction and carry the mucus with its trapped dust upwards to the pharynx, where it is swallowed or coughed out. This is often called the mucus escalator.

q: Which statement about the bronchioles is correct?
o: They are supported by complete rings of cartilage
Their walls have no cartilage but contain smooth muscle
They are lined by keratinised stratified epithelium
They open directly into the trachea
x: Bronchioles are narrow tubes without cartilage; smooth muscle in their walls can change their diameter. They branch from the bronchi, not directly from the trachea.

q: When the smooth muscle in the walls of the bronchioles contracts strongly, the result is:
o: Collapse of the trachea
Widening of the airways and easier breathing
Narrowing of the airways and more resistance to air flow
An increase in the surface area of the alveoli
x: Bronchioles have smooth muscle and no cartilage, so its contraction narrows them and makes breathing harder, as in an asthma attack. The trachea is held open by cartilage.

q: The walls of the alveoli are made of:
o: Plates of cartilage
Several layers of smooth muscle
A single layer of thin, flat (squamous) cells
Ciliated columnar cells
x: Each alveolus has a wall only one cell thick, made of flat squamous epithelium, which keeps the diffusion distance short. Ciliated cells and cartilage are found in the larger airways.

q: The correct path of air from the trachea to the gas-exchange surface is:
o: Trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveoli
Trachea → bronchioles → bronchi → alveolar ducts → alveoli
Trachea → alveolar ducts → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
Trachea → bronchi → alveolar ducts → bronchioles → alveoli
x: The trachea divides into two bronchi, which branch into ever smaller bronchioles. The finest bronchioles lead into alveolar ducts that end in clusters of alveoli.

q: The correct order of structures through which air passes when it is breathed in through the nose is:
o: Nasal cavity → larynx → pharynx → trachea
Pharynx → nasal cavity → larynx → trachea
Nasal cavity → pharynx → trachea → larynx
Nasal cavity → pharynx → larynx → trachea
x: Air enters the nasal cavity, passes back into the pharynx, then through the larynx (voice box) into the trachea. The larynx sits on top of the trachea.

q: Surfactant secreted on the inner surface of the alveoli is important because it:
o: Makes the alveoli contract during expiration
Kills all bacteria that reach the alveoli
Carries oxygen across the alveolar wall into the blood
Lowers surface tension, so the alveoli do not collapse
x: Surfactant reduces the surface tension of the watery film lining the alveoli, so they stay open and inflate easily. Oxygen crosses the wall by diffusion, not carried by surfactant.

q: Each lung is enclosed by a double membrane called the:
o: Peritoneum
Pleura
Meninges
Pericardium
x: The pleural membranes surround the lungs. The pericardium surrounds the heart, the peritoneum lines the abdomen and the meninges cover the brain and spinal cord.

q: The fluid in the pleural cavity, between the two pleural membranes, mainly:
o: Carries oxygen to the lung tissue
Reduces friction as the lungs move during breathing
Traps dust particles that reach the lungs
Stops the lungs from expanding too much
x: The thin layer of pleural fluid lubricates the membranes so they slide over each other smoothly as the lungs expand and recoil. It also helps the lungs follow the movement of the chest wall.

q: The diaphragm is a:
o: Bony plate that protects the lungs from below
Double membrane that covers the lungs
Cartilage flap that closes the larynx
Dome-shaped sheet of muscle separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities
x: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped muscular sheet forming the floor of the thoracic cavity. The pleura covers the lungs and the epiglottis closes the larynx.

q: During inspiration, the diaphragm:
o: Relaxes and moves downwards
Contracts and flattens, moving downwards
Relaxes and becomes more dome-shaped
Contracts and becomes more dome-shaped
x: Contraction pulls the dome of the diaphragm down and flattens it, which increases the vertical size of the thoracic cavity. During expiration it relaxes and returns to its dome shape.

q: During inspiration, contraction of the external intercostal muscles:
o: Pushes the diaphragm upwards
Compresses the lungs to force air out
Moves the ribs and sternum upwards and outwards
Moves the ribs downwards and inwards
x: The external intercostals pull the ribs up and out, widening the chest from front to back and side to side. This adds to the increase in thoracic volume caused by the diaphragm.

q: Which set of events occurs during normal inspiration?
o: Diaphragm contracts, thoracic volume increases, pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric
Diaphragm relaxes, thoracic volume increases, pressure in the lungs rises above atmospheric
Diaphragm contracts, thoracic volume decreases, pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric
Diaphragm relaxes, thoracic volume decreases, pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric
x: Contraction of the diaphragm (with the external intercostals) enlarges the thorax. The larger volume lowers the pressure inside the lungs below atmospheric pressure, so air flows in.

q: Normal quiet expiration is described as a passive process because it:
o: Results from relaxation of the breathing muscles and the elastic recoil of the lungs
Requires strong contraction of the abdominal muscles
Is controlled only by the cerebrum
Depends on the lungs actively pumping air out
x: In quiet breathing, the diaphragm and external intercostals simply relax and the stretched elastic lungs recoil, pushing air out. No extra muscle contraction is needed; abdominal muscles help only in forced expiration.

q: During forced expiration, such as blowing out hard, which muscles contract?
o: Smooth muscles of the alveoli
External intercostal muscles and the diaphragm
The diaphragm only
Internal intercostal muscles and abdominal wall muscles
x: Forced expiration uses the internal intercostals to pull the ribs down and in, and the abdominal muscles to push the abdominal organs up against the diaphragm. The diaphragm and external intercostals are inspiratory muscles.

q: The lungs have no muscles of their own. They expand during inspiration because:
o: The alveoli actively stretch themselves
The pressure inside the lungs rises above atmospheric pressure
The thoracic cavity enlarges, lowering the pressure inside the lungs
Air is pushed in by contraction of the trachea
x: The lungs follow the chest wall: as the diaphragm and intercostals enlarge the thorax, pressure in the lungs drops below atmospheric and air flows in, inflating them. Air moves from higher to lower pressure.

q: The respiratory centre that controls the basic rhythm of breathing is located in the:
o: Cerebellum
Medulla oblongata
Hypothalamus
Cerebral cortex
x: The respiratory centre lies in the medulla oblongata (helped by centres in the pons) of the brainstem. It sends impulses to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles. The cerebellum coordinates movement.

q: The rate and depth of breathing increase mainly in response to:
o: A rise in the oxygen level of the blood
A fall in the carbon dioxide level of the blood
A fall in body temperature
A rise in the carbon dioxide (and hydrogen ion) level of the blood
x: The respiratory centre is most sensitive to carbon dioxide: more CO2 makes the blood more acidic, and chemoreceptors then drive faster, deeper breathing. A fall in oxygen has a weaker effect in normal conditions.

q: Peripheral chemoreceptors that monitor blood gases and send impulses to the respiratory centre are found in the:
o: Kidneys
SA node and AV node
Alveolar walls
Carotid bodies and aortic bodies
x: Chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies (in the neck) and the aortic bodies (on the arch of the aorta) sense changes in CO2, H+ and O2 levels and signal the respiratory centre. The SA and AV nodes belong to the heart's conducting system.

q: During hard exercise the breathing rate rises. Which is the correct chain of events?
o: Muscles release more CO2 → blood becomes more acidic → chemoreceptors stimulate the respiratory centre → faster breathing
Blood CO2 falls → blood becomes more alkaline → respiratory centre is stimulated → faster breathing
Muscles use less oxygen → blood pH rises → diaphragm contracts more often → faster breathing
Blood oxygen rises → chemoreceptors are stimulated → respiratory centre is inhibited → faster breathing
x: Active muscles respire faster and release more CO2, which forms carbonic acid and lowers blood pH. Chemoreceptors detect this and the respiratory centre in the medulla increases the rate and depth of breathing.

q: A person cannot hold their breath indefinitely because:
o: Oxygen builds up in the blood and stimulates the respiratory centre
The diaphragm becomes permanently paralysed
Carbon dioxide builds up in the blood and stimulates the respiratory centre
The alveoli fill with mucus
x: While the breath is held, CO2 from respiration accumulates in the blood. The rising CO2 and acidity strongly stimulate the respiratory centre, which forces breathing to restart.

q: In the human lungs, exchange of gases between air and blood takes place across the walls of the:
o: Alveoli and the capillaries around them
Trachea
Bronchi
Pleural membranes
x: Gas exchange happens where the thin alveolar wall lies against the thin wall of a pulmonary capillary. The trachea and bronchi only conduct air, and the pleura surrounds the lungs.

q: Oxygen and carbon dioxide move between alveolar air and the blood by:
o: Pinocytosis by alveolar cells
Active transport using ATP
Osmosis through the alveolar wall
Simple diffusion down their partial pressure gradients
x: Each gas diffuses from where its partial pressure is higher to where it is lower. No energy is used; osmosis refers to water movement only.

q: Which feature does NOT help the alveoli carry out efficient gas exchange?
o: Walls only one cell thick
A dense network of capillaries around them
Cartilage present in their walls
A very large total surface area
x: Alveoli have no cartilage; it would only thicken the barrier. A large surface area, thin walls and many capillaries all speed up diffusion.

q: The inner surface of each alveolus is kept moist. This is important because:
o: Oxygen must dissolve in the moisture before it can diffuse across the wall
The moisture traps dust particles
The moisture prevents blood clotting in the capillaries
The moisture produces ATP for gas exchange
x: Gases cross cell membranes in solution, so oxygen first dissolves in the thin film of water lining the alveolus. Dust is trapped higher up the airways.

q: Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the pulmonary capillaries because:
o: The partial pressure of oxygen in the blood is higher than in alveolar air
Alveolar cells actively pump oxygen into the blood
The partial pressure of oxygen in alveolar air is higher than in the blood arriving at the lungs
Carbon dioxide leaving the blood pulls oxygen in with it
x: Blood arriving from the pulmonary artery is low in oxygen, so its pO2 is below that of alveolar air. Oxygen therefore diffuses down this gradient into the blood.

q: At sea level, atmospheric pressure is 760 mm Hg and air contains about 21% oxygen. The partial pressure of oxygen in atmospheric air is about:
o: 760 mm Hg
40 mm Hg
160 mm Hg
104 mm Hg
x: Partial pressure equals total pressure times the fraction of the gas: 0.21 × 760 ≈ 160 mm Hg. 760 mm Hg is the pressure of all the gases together.

q: Compared with atmospheric air, alveolar air has:
o: The same partial pressures of oxygen and carbon dioxide
Lower partial pressures of both oxygen and carbon dioxide
A lower partial pressure of oxygen and a higher partial pressure of carbon dioxide
A higher partial pressure of oxygen and a lower partial pressure of carbon dioxide
x: Alveolar air is a mixture of fresh air and air left in the lungs, and it constantly loses O2 to the blood and gains CO2 from it. So its pO2 is lower and its pCO2 higher than in atmospheric air.

q: Blood reaching the lungs has a pCO2 of about 45 mm Hg, while alveolar air has a pCO2 of about 40 mm Hg. Which statement is correct?
o: Carbon dioxide diffuses from the alveoli into the blood
No carbon dioxide moves because the gradient is too small
Carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli despite the small gradient
Carbon dioxide is actively transported into the alveoli
x: CO2 moves from higher to lower partial pressure, so from blood to alveoli. Even this small gradient is enough because carbon dioxide is far more soluble and diffuses much more readily than oxygen.

q: The blood carried to the lungs by the pulmonary arteries is:
o: High in oxygen and low in carbon dioxide
High in both oxygen and carbon dioxide
Low in oxygen and high in carbon dioxide
Low in both oxygen and carbon dioxide
x: The pulmonary arteries bring deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle, which has given O2 to the tissues and picked up CO2. In the lungs it gains O2 and loses CO2.

q: Most of the oxygen in the blood is transported:
o: Bound to plasma albumin
Dissolved in the plasma
As bicarbonate ions
Combined with haemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin
x: Nearly all oxygen in blood is carried by haemoglobin in red blood cells as oxyhaemoglobin; only a small amount dissolves in plasma. Bicarbonate is a form of carbon dioxide transport.

q: One molecule of haemoglobin can carry at most:
o: Four molecules of oxygen
Two molecules of oxygen
Eight molecules of oxygen
One molecule of oxygen
x: Haemoglobin has four polypeptide chains, each with one haem group containing one iron ion. Each haem binds one O2 molecule, so one haemoglobin carries up to four.

q: Oxygen binds to which part of the haemoglobin molecule?
o: The amino groups of the globin chains
The iron (Fe²⁺) ion in each haem group
A magnesium ion at the centre of the molecule
The membrane of the red blood cell
x: Each haem group has a ferrous iron ion that reversibly binds one oxygen molecule. The amino groups of globin are where carbon dioxide binds to form carbaminohaemoglobin; magnesium is found in chlorophyll.

q: In the body tissues, oxyhaemoglobin gives up its oxygen mainly because:
o: The partial pressure of oxygen in the tissues is high
The carbon dioxide level in the tissues is low
Haemoglobin is broken down in the tissues
The partial pressure of oxygen in the tissues is low
x: Respiring cells use oxygen, keeping tissue pO2 low. At low pO2 oxyhaemoglobin dissociates and the released oxygen diffuses into the cells.

q: In actively respiring muscle, the blood has more carbon dioxide and is more acidic. The effect of this on haemoglobin is that it:
o: Stops carrying carbon dioxide
Releases its oxygen more readily
Holds its oxygen more tightly
Picks up more oxygen from the plasma
x: High CO2 and acidity lower haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen (the Bohr effect), so more oxygen is unloaded exactly where it is most needed. This shifts the dissociation curve to the right.

q: Which change shifts the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve to the right, so that oxygen is released more easily?
o: A rise in temperature
A rise in blood pH
A fall in temperature
A fall in the partial pressure of carbon dioxide
x: Higher temperature, higher pCO2 and lower pH all reduce haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen and shift the curve to the right. A fall in pCO2, a rise in pH or a fall in temperature shift it to the left.

q: Carbon dioxide is carried in the blood in three forms. The largest share is carried as:
o: Carbaminohaemoglobin
Carbon dioxide dissolved in plasma
Carboxyhaemoglobin
Bicarbonate ions in the plasma
x: Most CO2 travels as bicarbonate ions (HCO3⁻) in the plasma. Smaller amounts are carried as carbaminohaemoglobin and dissolved CO2. Carboxyhaemoglobin is formed by carbon monoxide, not carbon dioxide.

q: Carbaminohaemoglobin is formed when carbon dioxide combines with:
o: The amino groups of the globin part of haemoglobin
The iron ions of the haem groups
Water in the plasma
Bicarbonate ions in the red blood cell
x: CO2 attaches to the amino groups of the globin chains, not to the iron, so it does not compete directly with oxygen for the haem. Combining with water forms carbonic acid instead.

q: The enzyme carbonic anhydrase speeds up the:
o: Reaction of carbon dioxide with water to form carbonic acid
Exchange of chloride ions across the red cell membrane
Binding of oxygen to haemoglobin
Formation of carboxyhaemoglobin
x: Carbonic anhydrase catalyses CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3, which then dissociates into H⁺ and HCO3⁻. Oxygen binding to haemoglobin needs no enzyme, and chloride moves through membrane channels.

q: The enzyme carbonic anhydrase is present in high concentration in:
o: Platelets
Lymphocytes
Blood plasma
Red blood cells
x: Carbonic anhydrase is found inside red blood cells, which is why carbonic acid forms rapidly there rather than in the plasma. The bicarbonate made in the cells then diffuses out into the plasma.

q: Inside red blood cells, carbonic acid dissociates into H⁺ and HCO3⁻ ions. Most of the H⁺ ions are then:
o: Released into the plasma, making it strongly acidic
Combined with chloride ions to form hydrochloric acid
Excreted straight into the alveoli
Buffered by combining with haemoglobin
x: Haemoglobin acts as a buffer by taking up H⁺ ions, which prevents a large fall in blood pH. The HCO3⁻ ions diffuse out into the plasma.

q: As bicarbonate ions diffuse out of red blood cells into the plasma, chloride ions move into the cells to balance the charge. This exchange is called the:
o: Bohr effect
Chloride shift
Oxygen debt
Osmotic shift
x: The chloride shift keeps the red cells electrically neutral as HCO3⁻ leaves. The Bohr effect is the drop in haemoglobin's oxygen affinity caused by CO2 and acidity.

q: In the lungs, bicarbonate is converted back into carbon dioxide. This conversion:
o: Produces oxygen, which enters the blood
Takes place inside red blood cells, and the CO2 released diffuses into the alveoli
Takes place in the alveolar air spaces
Takes place in the pleural fluid
x: In the pulmonary capillaries, HCO3⁻ re-enters the red cells, combines with H⁺ to form carbonic acid, and carbonic anhydrase splits it into CO2 and water. The CO2 then diffuses out into the alveoli.

q: Tidal volume is the volume of air:
o: Left in the lungs after the most forceful expiration
Breathed in or out in one normal, quiet breath
Held by the lungs after the deepest possible breath in
Breathed out forcefully after a deepest possible breath in
x: Tidal volume is the air moved in a single normal breath at rest. The other descriptions match vital capacity, residual volume and total lung capacity.

q: The tidal volume of a resting adult is about:
o: 500 mL
50 mL
x: At rest each normal breath moves about 500 mL (0.5 litre) of air. A volume around 5 litres is closer to the total capacity of the lungs.

q: Vital capacity is the:
o: Volume of air moved in one quiet breath
Maximum volume of air that can be breathed out after the deepest possible breath in
Volume of air that always remains in the lungs
Volume of air breathed per minute at rest
x: Vital capacity is the largest volume that can be moved in one breath: a maximal expiration after a maximal inspiration. It is the sum of tidal volume and the inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes.

q: The volume of air that remains in the lungs even after the most forceful expiration is the:
o: Inspiratory reserve volume
Tidal volume
Residual volume
Vital capacity
x: The residual volume can never be breathed out; it keeps the alveoli from collapsing and allows gas exchange to continue between breaths. Vital capacity is the air that can be breathed out.

q: A person has a tidal volume of 500 mL, an inspiratory reserve volume of 3000 mL and an expiratory reserve volume of 1100 mL. Their vital capacity is:
x: Vital capacity = tidal volume + inspiratory reserve volume + expiratory reserve volume = 500 + 3000 + 1100 = 4600 mL. Residual volume is not part of vital capacity.

q: A person's vital capacity is 4800 mL and their residual volume is 1200 mL. Their total lung capacity is:
x: Total lung capacity is the vital capacity plus the residual volume: 4800 + 1200 = 6000 mL. Subtracting the residual volume would give the wrong figure of 3600 mL.

q: Which of the following is NOT a part of the vital capacity?
o: Tidal volume
Inspiratory reserve volume
Residual volume
Expiratory reserve volume
x: Vital capacity includes tidal volume and both reserve volumes, because all of these can be breathed out. The residual volume stays in the lungs and is not included.

q: A person at rest breathes 16 times per minute with a tidal volume of 500 mL. The volume of air breathed in per minute is:
o: 16 litres
0.5 litre
4 litres
8 litres
x: Volume per minute = breaths per minute × tidal volume = 16 × 500 mL = 8000 mL, which is 8 litres.

q: Which statement about blood leaving the alveolar capillaries is correct?
o: It carries more carbon dioxide than when it arrived
Most of its haemoglobin is in the deoxygenated form
Its partial pressure of oxygen has risen to nearly equal that of alveolar air
Its partial pressure of oxygen is now higher than that of alveolar air
x: Diffusion continues until the blood's pO2 almost equals alveolar pO2; it cannot rise above it. The blood has lost CO2 and its haemoglobin is mostly oxyhaemoglobin.

q: The distance gases must diffuse between alveolar air and blood is very short because:
o: Cartilage holds the capillaries inside the alveolar air
The alveoli are lined with ciliated cells
Several layers of smooth muscle separate air from blood
The alveolar wall and the capillary wall are each only one cell thick and lie close together
x: Two thin layers of flat cells, pressed against each other, make a very short diffusion path. A short path, a large area and a steep gradient all speed up diffusion.

q: The addictive substance in tobacco smoke is:
o: Nicotine
Tar
Carbon monoxide
Ammonia
x: Nicotine acts on the nervous system and causes dependence, which is why smokers find it hard to stop. Tar carries most of the carcinogens, and carbon monoxide reduces oxygen transport.

q: Carbon monoxide in cigarette smoke reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood because it:
o: Paralyses the diaphragm
Combines with haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin
Destroys red blood cells in the alveoli
Blocks the alveoli with solid particles
x: Carbon monoxide binds to the haem of haemoglobin, forming carboxyhaemoglobin, so that haemoglobin can no longer carry oxygen. Solid particles in smoke make up tar, not carbon monoxide.

q: Compared with oxygen, carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin:
o: With exactly the same strength
Only in the absence of carbon dioxide
Much more weakly, so it is quickly released
Much more strongly, so it is not easily released
x: Haemoglobin's affinity for carbon monoxide is far greater than for oxygen, so carboxyhaemoglobin is stable and the haemoglobin stays blocked for a long time.

q: Most of the cancer-causing substances (carcinogens) in tobacco smoke are found in the:
o: Nicotine
Carbon monoxide
Water vapour
Tar
x: Tar is the sticky mixture of particles that settles in the airways and contains most of the carcinogens. Nicotine is addictive and carbon monoxide reduces oxygen transport.

q: Nicotine affects the circulation by:
o: Slowing the heart rate and lowering blood pressure
Raising the heart rate and narrowing blood vessels, which raises blood pressure
Widening all blood vessels in the body
Reducing the number of red blood cells
x: Nicotine stimulates the release of adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and constricts blood vessels. Together these raise blood pressure and add to the load on the heart.

q: In a regular smoker, the cilia lining the bronchi are paralysed and destroyed. The immediate result is that:
o: The cartilage rings of the bronchi dissolve
Mucus and trapped particles collect in the airways instead of being swept away
More air reaches the alveoli
Gas exchange in the alveoli becomes faster
x: Without beating cilia the mucus escalator stops, so mucus with dust and bacteria builds up in the airways. This leads to coughing and infections.

q: Tobacco smoke causes smokers to produce more mucus than normal because it:
o: Irritates the airway lining, so goblet cells and mucous glands secrete more mucus
Converts surfactant into mucus
Dissolves the cartilage of the bronchi
Destroys all the goblet cells of the trachea
x: Constant irritation by smoke makes goblet cells increase and mucous glands enlarge, so they secrete extra mucus. Combined with damaged cilia, this mucus collects in the airways.

q: A long-term smoker has a frequent cough, especially in the morning. This 'smoker's cough' is mainly because:
o: Coughing is the only way left to clear mucus that the damaged cilia cannot move
Nicotine directly paralyses the diaphragm
Carbon monoxide irritates the vocal cords
The alveoli fill with tar and burst
x: With the cilia destroyed, mucus collects in the bronchi, and the person has to cough to bring it up. This persistent cough is an early sign of chronic bronchitis.

q: Chronic bronchitis is a condition in which:
o: The bronchi are inflamed and produce excess mucus, causing a persistent cough
The walls of the alveoli break down
Cells in the lungs divide uncontrollably to form a tumour
The pleural membranes become inflamed
x: Chronic bronchitis is long-term inflammation of the bronchi, with too much mucus and a constant cough. Breakdown of alveolar walls is emphysema, and uncontrolled cell division is cancer.

q: In chronic bronchitis, breathing becomes difficult mainly because:
o: The trachea loses its cartilage rings
The alveoli become larger and more numerous
The diaphragm is paralysed
The bronchi are narrowed by inflammation and excess mucus
x: Swollen, inflamed bronchial walls and the mucus inside them narrow the airways, so it is harder to move air in and out. The disease affects the airways, not the diaphragm or tracheal cartilage.

q: Emphysema is a disease in which:
o: The walls between alveoli break down, forming fewer and larger air spaces
A tumour grows in the bronchus
The pleura fills with fluid
The bronchi become inflamed and full of mucus
x: In emphysema the thin walls between neighbouring alveoli are destroyed, so many small alveoli merge into fewer large spaces. Inflamed bronchi full of mucus describe bronchitis.

q: In emphysema, the rate of gas exchange falls mainly because:
o: The alveolar walls become many cells thick
The total surface area of the alveoli is greatly reduced
The number of red blood cells falls
The bronchi fill with tumour cells
x: When alveolar walls break down, many small alveoli become a few large spaces with much less total surface area, so less oxygen can diffuse into the blood. The person becomes breathless.

q: A person with emphysema finds it especially difficult to breathe out. This is because:
o: The diaphragm can no longer contract
The external intercostal muscles are paralysed
The lungs lose their elastic tissue, so they do not recoil properly during expiration
The trachea becomes blocked by cartilage
x: Quiet expiration depends on the elastic recoil of the lungs. In emphysema the elastic fibres are destroyed, so the lungs stay over-inflated and air is trapped; the problem is not the breathing muscles.

q: Smoke particles in the alveoli attract phagocytes. Enzymes released by these phagocytes digest the elastic fibres of the alveolar walls. This process leads to:
o: Pneumonia
Chronic bronchitis
Lung cancer
Emphysema
x: Digestion of elastic tissue and breakdown of alveolar walls is the cause of emphysema. Bronchitis is inflammation of the bronchi and lung cancer results from mutations.

q: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is the name used for the combination of:
o: Asthma and pneumonia
Emphysema and lung cancer
Lung cancer and tuberculosis
Chronic bronchitis and emphysema
x: COPD covers chronic bronchitis and emphysema, which often occur together in smokers and both obstruct air flow. Lung cancer and infections such as tuberculosis are separate diseases.

q: In smokers, lung cancer is caused mainly by:
o: Carbon monoxide binding to haemoglobin
Nicotine raising the heart rate
Shortage of oxygen in the lung tissue
Carcinogens in tar causing mutations in cells lining the airways
x: Carcinogens in tar damage the DNA of epithelial cells in the bronchi; when enough mutations build up, the cells divide uncontrollably and form a tumour. Carbon monoxide and nicotine have other harmful effects.

q: Lung cancer in smokers most often begins in the:
o: Epithelial cells lining the bronchi
Pleural membranes
Muscle of the diaphragm
Cartilage of the trachea
x: Tar settles on the lining of the bronchi, so its epithelial cells receive the most carcinogens and are where most lung cancers start. The pleura, diaphragm and cartilage are not directly exposed to smoke.

q: A lung tumour becomes much more dangerous when its cells:
o: Begin to produce antibodies
Stop dividing and become dormant
Spread through the blood or lymph to form tumours in other organs
Change back into normal epithelial cells
x: Spread of cancer cells to other parts of the body is called metastasis and makes the disease much harder to treat. Cancer cells do not change back into normal cells.

q: The risk of lung cancer rises with both the number of cigarettes smoked per day and the number of years of smoking. The best explanation is that:
o: Carbon monoxide accumulates in the lungs and forms a tumour
Longer and heavier exposure to carcinogens allows more mutations to build up in airway cells
Damaged cilia themselves turn into cancer cells
Nicotine slowly changes into a cancer cell
x: Cancer develops after several mutations accumulate in the same cell line. More cigarettes over more years means more exposure to the carcinogens in tar and a greater chance that this happens.

q: Which of the following is NOT an effect of tobacco smoke on the respiratory system?
o: An increase in the number of alveoli
Paralysis of the cilia
Excess secretion of mucus
Narrowing of the bronchi
x: Smoking damages cilia, increases mucus and narrows the bronchi. It does not add alveoli; in emphysema the number of alveoli actually falls as their walls break down.

q: Passive smoking means:
o: Smoking without inhaling into the lungs
Breathing in smoke from other people's cigarettes
Smoking cigarettes that have filters
Chewing tobacco instead of smoking it
x: Passive (second-hand) smoking is when non-smokers inhale smoke produced by smokers around them. They are exposed to the same harmful substances, though in smaller amounts.

q: Which compound is present in higher-than-normal amounts in the blood of a heavy smoker?
o: Plasma albumin
Oxyhaemoglobin
Surfactant
Carboxyhaemoglobin
x: Carbon monoxide from smoke combines with haemoglobin, so a smoker's blood contains more carboxyhaemoglobin and correspondingly less oxyhaemoglobin. Surfactant is found in the alveoli, not in blood.

q: Nicotine increases the risk of blood clots forming in the arteries because it:
o: Prevents fibrin from forming
Makes platelets stickier, so clots form more easily
Lowers the blood pressure
Destroys the platelets
x: Nicotine makes platelets more likely to stick together, raising the chance of a clot (thrombosis) in a narrowed artery. It raises, rather than lowers, blood pressure.

q: Smokers with chronic bronchitis suffer more lung infections because:
o: Nicotine kills all white blood cells
Mucus containing bacteria is not cleared, so the bacteria can multiply
Carbon monoxide feeds the bacteria
Tar removes the mucus that protects the airways
x: Damaged cilia cannot remove the extra mucus, which traps bacteria and gives them a warm, moist place to grow. Tar increases, not removes, mucus.

q: The main cause of lung cancer is:
o: Smoking tobacco
Drinking alcohol
Eating a high-salt diet
Lack of vitamin D
x: Tobacco smoking causes the large majority of lung cancers because of the carcinogens in tar. The other factors are not the main cause of lung cancer.

q: A woman who smokes during pregnancy supplies less oxygen to her fetus because of carbon monoxide in her blood. A well-known result is:
o: A rise in the fetus's oxygen supply
Lower birth weight of the baby
Higher birth weight of the baby
Faster growth of the fetal lungs
x: Carbon monoxide reduces the oxygen carried to the placenta and nicotine narrows blood vessels, so the fetus grows more slowly. Babies of smokers are on average smaller at birth.

q: Which statement correctly compares emphysema and chronic bronchitis?
o: Both are forms of lung cancer caused by tar
Emphysema is caused by bacteria, while chronic bronchitis is caused by nicotine
Emphysema mainly destroys the alveoli, while chronic bronchitis mainly affects the bronchi
Emphysema mainly affects the bronchi, while chronic bronchitis mainly destroys the alveoli
x: Emphysema is damage to the gas-exchange surface (alveolar walls), while chronic bronchitis is inflammation and excess mucus in the bronchi. Neither is cancer, though both are linked to smoking.

q: Which damage caused by smoking cannot be repaired after the person stops smoking?
o: Breakdown of the alveolar walls in emphysema
The raised heart rate caused by nicotine
The carboxyhaemoglobin present in the blood
The extra adrenaline released in response to nicotine
x: Destroyed alveolar walls do not grow back, so emphysema is permanent. The effects of nicotine on heart rate and adrenaline wear off, and carbon monoxide is gradually released from haemoglobin after smoking stops.

q: In emphysema, air becomes trapped in the lungs. Compared with a healthy person, a person with emphysema has a:
o: Smaller residual volume and a larger vital capacity
Larger residual volume and a larger vital capacity
Larger residual volume and a smaller vital capacity
Smaller residual volume and a smaller vital capacity
x: Loss of elastic recoil means more air stays in the lungs after expiration, so residual volume rises. Less air can then be moved in one breath, so vital capacity falls.

q: Which statement about nicotine is correct?
o: It is addictive and is quickly absorbed into the blood from the lungs
It is the solid particulate part of smoke that blackens the lungs
It is the main carcinogen in tobacco smoke
It binds to haemoglobin in place of oxygen
x: Nicotine passes rapidly from the alveoli into the blood and reaches the brain, causing addiction. The carcinogens and black deposits come from tar, and carbon monoxide is what binds haemoglobin.

q: Examination of a long-term smoker shows few cilia in the bronchi, enlarged mucous glands and a constant cough that brings up mucus. These findings are typical of:
o: Lung cancer
Asthma
Chronic bronchitis
Emphysema
x: Loss of cilia, overgrown mucous glands and a productive cough are the features of chronic bronchitis, which affects the bronchi. Emphysema is defined by damage to the alveoli.
